scenes.heading: Event-Driven Messaging with Kafka & NATS
scenes.narration: Event-driven architecture replaces brittle synchronous RPC chains with asynchronous messages. Let's see how Kafka and NATS decouple your services in time.

scenes.heading: Async over synchronous RPC
items: A producer publishes an event and returns immediately
Consumers process it whenever they're ready
A down consumer no longer fails the producer
scenes.narration: In synchronous RPC the caller blocks until the callee replies, so a slow or down dependency propagates failure upstream. Event-driven messaging inverts this: a producer writes an event to a durable broker and returns immediately, and consumers process it whenever they are ready. That decouples services in time, absorbs traffic spikes in the log, and lets each side scale independently.

scenes.heading: Kafka's core model
steps: A topic is an append-only log split into partitions
Each record gets a monotonic offset
The message key hashes to a partition
Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition
A consumer group splits partitions across members
scenes.narration: Kafka models a topic as an append-only log split into partitions, and each record in a partition gets a monotonically increasing offset. The producer's message key is hashed to pick a partition, so all events for the same key stay together and stay ordered — but ordering is guaranteed only within a single partition. A consumer group then splits those partitions across its members for parallel processing.

scenes.heading: At-least-once with idempotency
scenes.narration: Most real systems run at-least-once: a consumer might process a message and crash before committing its offset, so on restart it reprocesses. So you fetch without auto-commit, dedupe by a stable event ID, do the work, and commit the offset only after processing succeeds. That way a redelivered message is silently skipped and a crash before commit replays safely. Assume duplicates, and make replaying an event harmless.

scenes.text: NATS core is fire-and-forget pub/sub; JetStream adds durable streams with acks and redelivery.
scenes.narration: NATS gives you a spectrum. NATS core is lightweight pub/sub over hierarchical subjects, but it's fire-and-forget: if no subscriber is listening, the message is gone. JetStream layers durability on top, persisting messages into streams and redelivering any that aren't acknowledged — giving you Kafka-like at-least-once guarantees with a much simpler operational footprint.

scenes.text: Watch consumer lag — it's the primary health signal; scale out up to the partition count.
scenes.narration: Finally, watch consumer lag, the gap between the newest offset and what your group has committed. It's the primary health signal of an event-driven system: rising lag means consumers can't keep up, and you respond by scaling out consumers up to the partition count, speeding up per-message work, or adding partitions.
